Distracted, unable to think,
Kongurbay rushed inside.
“I shall die before my appointed death,” he said,
Kongurbay fled inside.
Stepping through the gateway,
Then he went
Before Esenkan,
Speaking ill of wretched me:
“He will not let our work proceed.
That bastard-piss creature of Azizkan,
He will not let us stay in Beijing!
He will plunder the gold,
He will bring us torment.
If you do not restrain this pig,
If you do not cut off his apple-round head,
He will scatter vast amounts of gold.
If the mood takes him, refusing allegiance,
He will flee toward the Burut!
Me, great as a mountain,
He unhorsed six times,
Killing me before my time.
He nearly gouged out
My two eyes, clear as glass.
Well, let him stay in Beijing;
I shall not turn Algara's head back.
As khan of the monks,
I shall not remain on the frontier!
This son of Azizkan,
When he reaches fifteen, will leave no peace.
We shall load our goods on mules.
Just watch, Esenkan,
From that bastard-piss pig
We shall suffer havoc!
He will not let us yoke a plow-team,
He will not let us sow two handfuls of grain.
If he unleashes his wrath,
The Chinese, that teeming people,
He will make them cower in Beijing;
He will not let them move a handspan.
The reason he will not let them move:
Sarala beneath him,
He came having saddled him, I heard.
Every language of the dragon
He came having learned, I heard.”
Saying this, Kongurbay
Carried out what he had said.
From before Esenkan,
Kalcha fled away.
Unaware of that dog's conduct,
Without heeding what he said,
I turned my head toward the khan,
And petitioned Esenkan:
“Of the Chinese people of forty khans,
Give me one khanship,” I said.
That was what I stood demanding.
“Give me the Sibe khanship,” I said.
“I gave it to Orokkyr,” he said,
Thus disappointing me.
When I asked for the Manchu khanship,
“I gave it to Ezkara,” he said,
Again disappointing me.
“Give me the Solon khanship,” I said.
“I gave it to Börüköz,” he said.
When I asked for the Torgut khanship,
“I gave it to Kanyshay,” he said.
When I asked for the Kalmyk khanship,
“I gave it to Khan Zholoy,” he said.
When I asked for the governors' khanship,
“I gave it to the lama,” he said.
When I asked for the monks' khanship,
“I gave it to Kongurbay,” he said.
When I asked for the one-eyed people's khanship,
“I gave it to Great Malgun,” he said.
His scalp drew tight,
May it strike your head, Esenkan,
As he quarreled with me.
“My child, your age this year
Has not yet reached twelve.
Your mind is not yet full of wisdom.
Your fledgling feathers are not full-grown,
Your childhood has not left you.
Your time to be khan has not come,
Your head is not yet full of brains.
You are an unfinished witless thing;
For now you are a child.
You have come before me.
Know that I am khan,” he said,
“Wear an official's stone,” he said.
Since I was the son of a lesser khan,
How could I heed his words?
Scorning the official's stone as mere stone,
With what face could I wear it?
Among the Chinese people of forty khans,
Not equal to a single khan,
Think of this, Manas:
How could I keep living?
I took my sword in hand.
In Kakan-Chin's Beijing,
Then I, Almambet,
Truly brought terror.
I turned Sarala's head.
That mighty khan Esenkan,
To slaughter him if he came outside,
I lay in wait for eight days.
What can I do in this sorrowful world?
Sarala was too well-fed;
Beijing's khan Esenkan,
His hour of death had not arrived.
Had Esenkan fallen into my hands,
Would I not have tested then
Sarala, the swift noble steed?
Had I met Esenkan,
Cutting off his single head,
Would I not have brought upon Beijing
An uproar no human had heard?
Esenkan in the palace,
While I was watching for him,
I saw a beauty among women,
She herself a young child,
Not yet twelve years old,
Thimble-mouthed, with a young camel's eyes,
I saw so beautiful a girl.
When I saw that girl,
My heart caught fire.
“She is exceptional,” in Beijing,
“Burulcha,” I had been saying.
When I saw such beauty,
“Let khanship sink into the earth!
By becoming khan in Beijing,
What desire would I fulfill?
Esenkan's daughter Burulcha,
If she will heed my words,
Let me take her as my bride!”
I struck Sarala once on the thigh.
Esenkan's daughter Burulcha,
I put my hand to her breast.
She would not agree to what I said.
Her breast—Burulcha would not
Agree to let me hold it.
Though I said I would make her my bride,
She did not give me her heart.
Then the girl Burulcha said this:
“Find a land beyond the turning,
If you are pure, Almambet,
Find a people among the Muslims.
When you become a true Muslim,
Then I shall marry you.
Become clean of the dark faith,
Flee the unbelievers and become a stranger to them.
Until you turn back and return,
Until I see your fair face,
Let me bind my black hair.
‘Almambet who went to Islam,
When will he return safely?’ I shall say,
And keep waiting for you.
If fate brings us together,
Let me put my arms around your neck.
If Islam is an evil faith,
Tomorrow, on Judgment Day,
Becoming a black donkey then,
Let me bear your torment.
You were a son of light,
I was a daughter of light.
From that time until this,
You never pause and sit down;
You do not know the Muslim faith.
Almambet, you are bare ground where horses are tethered,
Fashioning it with your hands,
Calling bronze a god,
You are an unbeliever who knows no faith.
If you become a Muslim and take me,
My hero, to you yourself,
My very head is a sacrifice.
However many unbelieving khans gather,
Almambet has ridden here.
Let them be sacrifices to my hem!”
Saying this, Burulcha
Made my misfortune bitter.
She jerked, shook and flung away
My hand upon her breast.
Burulcha spoke a word;
She put a defiling word into my heart.
When I heard Burulcha's words,
Unable to go, I staggered.
I had no thought of becoming Muslim.
“This young girl, this calamity,
What is she saying?” I said,
And marveled to myself.
“His daughter too has become an enemy,” I said.
My insides burned to embers
From the torment of this girl.
Burulcha stopped at that.
The double-edged hard steel,
Seizing it by the hilt,
I drew out of its sheath.
When I took the sword in hand,
Esenkan's Burulcha,
When she had stirred much turmoil,
To cut off her head,
I lunged and reached her.
Burulcha fled screaming.
He whose fortune had not left him,
Whom forty warriors could not match,
Esenkan's, then,
Gate made of iron,
When I struck it with the sword,
Shattered into fragments.
When she saw my fierce wrath,
Into Esenkan's palace
She fled screaming.
Enough, leopard Manas,
When I had reached twelve,
I let Sarala grow lean.
Esenkan and Kongurbay,
Driving the two of them then,
I put them to flight from Outer Beijing.
When they were caught in captivity,
Esenkan escaped
And went to Karykan.
“He slaughtered Outer Beijing's people,” he said,
Speaking ill of me to Karykan,
He spread tales about me.
These words he spoke,
Karykan in Beijing
Believed, and was thrown into panic.
May God never show its face:
In Kakan-Chin's Beijing
He issued a great command.
However many giants and mighty men there were,
He gathered them, sparing none.
Let me name the mighty men:
The giant Kutan, whose ears were iron,
The giant Mangküsh, whose forehead was iron,
His Kalmyk, the Great Lama,
His champion like Great Zholoy.
Thus upon Beijing,
Because of wretched me,
An uproar descended.
A thousand swift runners
Came up through the narrow passage.
A thousand dagger-handed men
Came surrounding us.
All those mighty men:
“See the khan's command,” they said,
“Your twelve-year-old child,
Give him to us now,” they said,
And kept surrounding us.
The Chinese gathered about the khan,
Since they would not be satisfied,
“This is the khan's command,” they said.
The many Chinese who came besieging,
With my father the khan, one like me
They would not leave.
